newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French tax cuts fail to lift consumer gloom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French tax cuts fail to lift consumer gloom.

text.p: French consumers gave a dark assessment of the economy in a survey released on Thursday which showed government promises of tax cuts have failed to convince them that things are getting better.

A survey conducted by national statistics institute INSEE in September showed household confidence had slid yet again and fears for jobs had risen despite a tax-cutting package meant to encourage consumer spending and give the economy a lift.

Economists said the survey had to be treated with scepticism because other data showed consumer spending was actually rising -- but they said it proved in stark political terms how badly Prime Minister Alain Juppe was faring in the eyes of the public.
"It's a very good indicator that the government is just not supported," said Eric Chaney, Paris economist at U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley.

Chaney and other economists said there was plenty of evidence that consumers were spending more on cars and homes and that the economy was starting to benefit, but the "feel-bad" measure tended to lag reality.
"I'd say it's just a measure of government popularity," said Philippe Brossard, ABN Amro's French economy specialist.

Data released last month showed spending rose a hefty 3.0 percent in August on the back of car sales buoyed by government incentives. Spending also rose in other areas and is expected to bolster economic growth in the third quarter of the year.

Historically, the household confidence survey shows people feel much better at election time because of campaign promises and their views tend to darken later, whatever the trend in actual spending, the economists said.

INSEE, whose confidence survey was conducted from September 2 to 21, said its overall index of consumer sentiment fell to minus 37 in September from 35 in July. There is no survey in August, when most French people traditionally go on holiday.
Consumer views on the outlook for unemployment worsened, showing a level of 79 for those expecting joblessness to rise, compared to 77 in July and just 30 in October 1995.
The overall confidence index does not take account of the feelings on unemployment. Unemployment reached a record 12.6 percent in August, hitting 3.09 million people.

Juppe's tax package announced in early September includes net income tax cuts of 18 billion francs ($3.47 billion) next year to offset the impact on the economy of spending cuts unveiled in the 1997 budget later in the month.
The package seems to have done more for confidence in the financial markets than among the wider electorate.
The tax cut plans were widely attacked in the French press, which said other increases on excise duties and local authority taxes would minimise the impact of the tax cuts.
INSEE's overall confidence index hit a trough of minus 38 in May this year compared to minus 30 in October last year.
The overall index covers views on past and future living standards, past and future personal finances and whether people think it is a good time to spend.
Chaney said the real implication was that Juppe desperately needed to be able to show the economy really was picking up but the statistical proof would come after the event.
With the government likely to start preparing for 1998 parliamentary elections early next year, Juppe needed proof of success if he wanted to stay on, he said.

For now, however, Juppe's place is seens as safe. He is identified with France's commitment to European monetary union and President Jacques Chirac is unlikely to want to change that ahead of a crucial summit of EU leaders in Dublin in December. ($1=5.181 French Franc)
